rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 6 compounds and map the overall elution window while reducing risk of truncation. This should reveal whether peaks are compressed early, held late, or reasonably distributed, guiding the next window and slope adjustments.

The first run started at too high phi0, leaving four compounds essentially unretained at the dead time. Drop phi0 to the minimum while keeping phi1 and tG broad so the early cluster moves into the gradient and we can see whether low-start retention alone resolves the critical pairs.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only leverage is reducing t_last. Halve tG first while keeping the same window and temperature to test how much run time can be cut before any pair approaches the 1.5 resolution threshold.

We have full resolution with margin and t_last under 10 min, so now probe whether the gradient can be shortened further without any pair dropping below R = 1.5. The current worst pair is still very safe, making a 2 min reduction the next efficient step.

Resolution remains comfortably above threshold after shortening to 8 min, so continue stepping down tG to find the shortest gradient that still keeps every adjacent pair at R at least 1.5. The early pair is the limiting one, and this run will show how close we are to the edge.

The worst pair still has good margin at tG 6 min, so shorten once more to locate the practical minimum gradient time before the first pair falls under full-credit resolution. This directly optimizes the shortest fully resolved method, which is the scoring target.

At tG 4 min the limiting pair is just above full-credit resolution, so the next step is to test the shortest allowed gradient. This will tell us whether 2 min still preserves R at least 1.5 for all pairs, potentially giving the fastest optimal method.

tG 4 min is the shortest fully resolved method so far, and the only vulnerable pair is the first one. Narrowing the gradient window slightly at the high end should make the slope shallower without sacrificing elution, potentially preserving full resolution while giving room to optimize further around the same short run.

Lowering phi1 at tG 4 min improved the limiting pair, so now retest the 2 min gradient with the shallower 0.05 to 0.90 window. If full resolution is retained, this would beat the current shortest optimal method.

The limiting first pair improved again when phi1 was lowered from 0.95 to 0.90 at tG 2 min, so continue narrowing the high end to further reduce gradient steepness. This directly tests whether a 2 min method can be brought back to full-credit resolution without changing the low-start condition that is clearly needed.

The 2 min run keeps improving as phi1 is lowered, and all compounds still elute very early, so there is room to keep narrowing the window. This tests whether further reducing steepness can lift the first pair to full-credit resolution while maintaining a very short analysis.

The limiting pair continues to improve monotonically as phi1 decreases, and the last peak is still very early, so one more reduction in phi1 is the most direct way to see whether the 2 min method can cross R = 1.5. This keeps the same low phi0 that is essential for retaining the earliest compounds.

The first pair is still the sole limiter and keeps gaining resolution as the gradient window narrows, while the last peak remains well within the run. Continue lowering phi1 to determine whether the 2 min method can reach full-credit separation before late-elution risk appears.

The 2 min gradient is still improving steadily as phi1 drops, and the last peak at phi1 0.70 is only 4.25 min, so there is still room to narrow the window. This is the most informative next step to see if the limiting pair can approach or exceed R = 1.5 while staying comfortably under the 10 min cutoff.

The first pair keeps responding favorably to a narrower 2 min gradient, and the last peak is still comfortably before 10 min, so another step down in phi1 is justified. This is the fastest route to determine whether the 2 min method can finally reach R >= 1.5 for every pair.

At phi1 0.60 and tG 2 min the only remaining shortfall is the first pair, now quite close to full-credit resolution, suggesting slope is nearly sufficient and selectivity may need a temperature shift. A lower temperature is worth testing because it often changes close-pair selectivity while retention is still comfortably within the 10 min target.

Lower temperature fixed the critical pair but pushed the last peak just past 10 min, so the best next move is a partial step back up in temperature to balance selectivity and speed. Testing 30 C should show whether we can keep all pairs above R = 1.5 while bringing t_last back under the scoring threshold.

30 C gives a perfect score with comfortable resolution, and 40 C was too hot for the first pair, so 35 C is the key bracket point to locate the highest temperature that still keeps all pairs at full credit. If it succeeds, it should be a faster optimal method than 30 C.

At 35 C the 2 min method is still fully resolved with the limiting pair just above threshold, so narrowing the window one more step should increase that margin while likely remaining under 10 min for the last peak. This probes whether we can make the shortest optimal method more robust without sacrificing the perfect score.

The current best region is phi1 0.60, tG 2 min, where 35 C and 30 C are perfect and 40 C loses only on the first pair. Testing 50 C checks whether the late compound can be sped up enough to support a still narrower window or whether selectivity collapses too much, sharpening our understanding of the temperature tradeoff around the optimum.

The best zone is bracketed: 35 C is fully resolved, while 40 C and 50 C lose the first pair. Testing 45 C tightens that temperature boundary and confirms whether 35 C is indeed the highest temperature that preserves a perfect score at the shortest 2 min gradient.

The optimum appears to lie at phi1 0.60 with 30–35 C, and higher temperature clearly erodes the critical first-pair selectivity. A 60 C point completes the temperature map at the shortest gradient, confirming the monotonic loss and closing off any remaining chance that extreme heating could offset the resolution loss with a different selectivity regime.

We have already found perfect-score 2 min methods, but among the perfect-score set the shortest actual run is 2 min at 35 C; still, testing 4 min at the same window and temperature checks whether the late compound stays well under 10 min while greatly increasing robustness of the critical pair. This is a final confirmation of the local optimum region and whether the phi1 0.60 window behaves predictably with a shallower slope at the best temperature band.

At tG 2 min, 35 C is perfect while 40 C fails on the first pair, so increasing tG to 4 min may allow 40 C to recover full resolution and still keep t_last under 10 min. This tests whether a hotter, slightly longer gradient can match the perfect score while offering a useful alternative optimum near the time threshold.

A final point at 4 min and 45 C will complete the boundary between the successful 4 min, 40 C method and the failed 2 min, 45 C method. This checks whether a slightly hotter fully resolved method exists at the same short window, but the current best remains the 2 min methods at 30–35 C.
